article_title: Delivering virtual K-8 computing professional development in rural KY
citation: Iwatani, E., Tackett, T., Ruiz, P., & Burke, Q. (2021). Delivering Virtual K-8 Computing Professional Development in Rural KY. Digital Promise / Bit Source. https://bit.ly/36szXLy
title: CT Booster session structure: timed segments for vocabulary, examples, micro-credentials, and Q&A
description: Each CT Booster session follows a repeating timed structure: a short introduction and vocabulary segment, a set of worked examples anchored by guiding questions, a pointer to a related micro-credential, and a closing question-and-answer period. The deck prints the structure as "5-10 minutes: Introduction & Vocabulary" followed by "15-20 minutes: 3-4 Examples" and "2-5 minutes: Question & Answer Session". Guiding questions frame the examples, for example how teachers collect, analyze, and store data to understand relationships in intermediate and middle grades.
requirements: Sessions need prepared example sets (3-4 examples) matched to a guiding question and a related micro-credential to point teachers toward
constraints: Structure is designed for short virtual booster sessions, not full-length courses
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking: data analysis and algorithms
examples: The K-2 Data & Analysis session on November 10, 2020 and the 3-8 Algorithms session on January 19, 2021 both used this timed structure

article_title: Educating Teachers in California: What Matters for Teacher Preparedness?
citation: Patrick, S. K., Darling-Hammond, L., & Kini, T. (2023). Educating teachers in California: What matters for teacher preparedness? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/956.678
title: CTC teacher preparation program completer survey system
description: A statewide survey system administered by the California Commission on Teacher Credentialing since 2016–17, embedded in the online preliminary credential application so that "the survey responses across all years are high." Between 2016–17 and 2020–21, "59,140 completers from 107 different California TPPs responded to the survey." constraints: It excludes California TPP completers who never applied for a preliminary credential in California and teachers prepared out of state; response rates for CSU completers must be estimated because CSU's data system does not track respondents

target_learning_goals: assessing completer preparedness across the teaching performance expectations
supporting program accreditation and continuous improvement
examples: Survey results are integrated into a public data dashboard showing statewide trends, while institution-level results are available to programs to support programmatic improvement

article_title: Warning About AI Fallibility Increases Help-Seeking in an Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Mirella Hladký, and Vera Rief. (2026). Warning About AI Fallibility Increases Help-Seeking in an Intelligent Tutoring System. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03822
title: Math intelligent tutoring system with fox-shaped pedagogical agent Maddox and rule-based hard-coded hints
description: A math intelligent tutoring system built with the Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools to support secondary students practicing systems of linear equations. Students begin with "drag-and-drop manipulations, selecting the next strategic step from a set of predefined options" and later move to free-text input. A fox-shaped pedagogical agent, Maddox, provides hints and targeted feedback that are "rule-based and hard-coded, without reliance on LLM-generated responses." The study compared two versions differing only in the popup message shown.
requirements: Requires the Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools for authoring
hints and feedback must be hard-coded to guarantee identical system behavior across conditions
constraints: The system deliberately contains no errors or LLM-generated content
so the warning concerns fallibility that is not actually present
target_learning_goals: solving systems of linear equations using substitution, equalization, and elimination methods
examples: Students practiced three solution methods across two interface versions during two 50-minute class periods

citation: Shile Zhang and Shuhan Zhang. (2026). Integrating AI into computational thinking: development and validation of an assessment tool for higher education students. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00623-0
title: CTAT student model: four CT constructs aligned with the AI training process
description: The CTAT student model specifies four CT constructs — Data, Conditionals, Loops, and Testing and Debugging — as the focal knowledge, skills, and abilities measured in an AI training context. It combines Brennan and Resnick's CT concepts-and-practices framework with Tedre et al.'s CT 2.0 framework, which "brings in data-driven and AI-related practices". The article states: "As a result, four CT constructs were selected: Data, Conditionals, Loops, and Testing and Debugging, which align with the AI training process". Each construct is broken into measurable FKSAs, and constructs are sequenced to match AI training stages from data preparation to testing and debugging.
requirements: Each FKSA is measured independently by items without overlap
Items must differ in complexity to reflect different competency levels
constraints: Designed for higher education students in CS- and AI-related majors with prior text-based programming knowledge
target_learners: Higher education students in computer sciences and AI-related programs
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking concepts and practices in AI training contexts
examples: The constructs align with China's Artificial Intelligence Innovation Action Plan for Colleges and Universities and updated ISTE AI-related learning standards

title: CTAT: Computational Thinking in AI Training Test
description: CTAT is a validated multiple-choice assessment of computational thinking in AI training contexts for higher education CS/AI students, developed using Evidence-Centered Design. Items use a notebook-style Python interface with schematic diagrams and visual symbols to reduce literacy and code-comprehension barriers, and combine AI model training tasks with text-based programming.

Each item maps to a single FKSA with one correct answer and three distractors
constraints: Intended for CS- and AI-related major students; test information peaks for slightly above-average ability students

target_learning_goals: CT concepts and practices including data handling, conditionals, loops, and testing and debugging in AI training

citation: Papaneophytou, C.; Nicolaou, S.A. (2025). Promoting Critical Thinking in Biological Sciences in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Higher Education. Trends High. Educ. 2025, 4, 24. https://doi.org/10.3390/higheredu4020024
title: Critical thinking as purposeful, self-regulatory judgment with cognitive skills and dispositions (Facione Delphi framework and Ennis definition)
description: The review organizes critical thinking around two established definitions. Facione's Delphi Report defines CT as "purposeful, self-regulatory judgment" involving interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, and explanation, plus dispositions such as open-mindedness, inquisitiveness, and truth-seeking. Ennis defines CT as "reasonable reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do" and emphasizes its teachability through direct instruction, practice, and feedback. The review applies these frameworks to AI-mediated learning in biology, arguing students need reflective tendencies to question and ethically evaluate AI-generated information.
requirements: Instruction must embed CT across disciplines through direct instruction, practice, and feedback, as Ennis advocates
constraints: The review notes CT is cultivated through experiential learning rather than direct instruction alone, embodying a lifestyle of active engagement with information
target_learners: undergraduate biological sciences students in higher education
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills and dispositions for scientific inquiry and evaluation of AI-generated information
examples: The review lists Delphi cognitive skills: analysis, inference, evaluation, plus interpretation, explanation, and self-regulation

article_title: Effectiveness of Critical Thinking Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Intervention Studies
citation: Dawit T. Tiruneh, An Verburgh & Jan Elen. (2014). Effectiveness of Critical Thinking Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Intervention Studies. Higher Education Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/hes.v4n1p1
title: Ennis's four-approach taxonomy of critical thinking instruction: general, infusion, immersion, and mixed
description: The review adopts Ennis's (1989) taxonomy organizing CT instruction into four approaches. In the general approach, CT is taught separately from subject matter; the infusion approach integrates CT instruction in subject matter while making general CT principles explicit; the immersion approach embeds CT in subjects without making principles explicit; and the mixed approach combines the general approach with infusion or immersion, with a separate thread teaching general CT principles alongside subject-specific CT instruction. The review uses this taxonomy to categorize all 33 included studies.
requirements: CT skills must be identifiable and definable as domain-independent skills that can be taught and transferred
constraints: The review notes the associated assumption that domain-independent thinking skills can be taught and transferred to daily-life situations
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills and dispositions
examples: All 33 studies were categorized: general approach 5 studies (15%), infusion 9 (27%), immersion 16 (49%), mixed 3 (9%)

title: Web-based erroneous examples and problem-solving lessons for decimals built with CTAT
description: Two 36-item web-based lessons (erroneous examples and problem solving) were implemented with the Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools (CTAT), whose "behavior graphs" model correct solution paths and typical errors; decimal misconceptions were represented as errors in these graphs. Erroneous example items walked students through reviewing, identifying, fixing, and explaining a fictional student's error, with green/red and text feedback. description: Because no Portuguese test assessed critical thinking for basic school students, the authors built the CTTBE from the national Profile of Students at the End of Compulsory Schooling, with items reviewed by two experts for relevance and clarity. article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Translate CTA findings into training, protocols, and knowledge transfer for practitioners
description: The article recommends that researchers applying CTA consider how findings can provide evidence-based insights into how experts carry out workplace activities and be translated into recommendations for improving decision-making and performance. Findings can "be used to translate expert knowledge into training and protocols", offering detailed documentation of complex cognitive processes used by skilled practitioners in situ — an approach described as especially fruitful in medical training, aviation, and the military. Having individuals reflect on their decision-making during critical tasks can improve future performance and facilitate knowledge transfer.
requirements: Findings must yield insights into cognitive challenges and the role of expertise, not merely a compelling story of workplace activities
Working directly with end-users to build collaborative relationships
constraints: Some authors describe a crisis in organizational science where statistically sophisticated methods fail to offer meaningful utility to practitioners — CTA is positioned as a response to this
target_learners: Practitioners, technical specialists, HR practitioners, and trainees in complex work domains
target_learning_goals: Knowledge transfer of expert cognition; improved decision-making and performance
examples: Cognitive Demands Tables represent challenges, errors, and solutions to inform future training and job design

citation: Yadav, A., Hong, H., & Stephenson, C. (2016). Computational Thinking for All: Pedagogical Approaches to Embedding 21st Century Problem Solving in K-12 Classrooms. TechTrends. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-016-0087-7
title: Computational thinking as three key constructs: algorithms, abstraction, and automation
description: The article organizes computational thinking around what Wing (2006) called the three key constructs. It states that "An algorithm (much like a recipe) is a step-by-step series of instructions," that abstraction "involves generalizing and transferring the problem solving process to similar problems," and that automation "involves using digital and simulation tools to mechanize problem solutions." These constructs are presented as foundational to computer science yet applicable across disciplines, framing the article's argument for embedding CT in K-12 content areas.

constraints: The article presents the constructs as an argumentative framework rather than a tested model

article_title: Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers’ video analysis
citation: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning as a design framework for novice video analysis
description: The article uses the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML; Mayer, 2001) as the guiding framework for designing novice-supportive video-analysis training. It states that the theory "assumes: (1) visual and auditory information is processed through separate channels; (2) each channel is limited in the amount of processing that can take place at once; and (3) learning occurs through active processing which involves information selection, organization into mental representations, and knowledge integration". The study maps two training techniques onto this framework: signaling cues for the information-selection step and principle-based self-explanation prompts for knowledge integration.
requirements: novices with limited prior knowledge whose processing capacity must be protected, per the article's statement that designers should "mitigate the challenges associated with different representations and modalities"
constraints: the article ties the framework's support techniques to transient information presentation, noting video learning "can be difficult due to the transient nature of information presentation"
target_learners: preservice teachers with limited prior knowledge and teaching experience
target_learning_goals: professional vision skill development in analyzing teaching practice
examples: The study operationalized selection support with integrated keyword cues and integration support with focused self-explanation prompts in a one-week video analysis training.

article_title: There’s more to the multimedia effect than meets the eye: is seeing pictures believing?
citation: Ögren, M., Nyström, M., & Jarodzka, H. (2017). There's more to the multimedia effect than meets the eye: is seeing pictures believing? Instructional Science, 45, 263–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9397-6
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Cognitive Load Theory as explanatory frameworks for learning with text and pictures
description: The article applies two leading theories of multimedia processing — the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Cognitive Load Theory — which assign a central role to a capacity-limited working memory. Active processing proceeds in three steps: information is "selected from a source by means of attention", organized into mental models, and integrated with each other and prior knowledge. Working memory load comprises germane, intrinsic, and extraneous load, and verbal and pictorial information are processed in separate channels that are later integrated into a richer mental model. The study adapts these learning-oriented principles to task performance in vector calculus and tests their predictions with eye tracking and think-aloud protocols.
requirements: Graphs must be carefully integrated with the task formulation so that students actively select, organize, and integrate information rather than process it shallowly
constraints: The article notes the study's stimuli followed the temporal contiguity principle but not the spatial contiguity principle (split attention), which may partly explain the absence of a multimedia effect

The authors state the experiment did not precisely reflect how students normally work with such problems: time was limited, no pen and paper was allowed, and the confirm/reject answer format was uncommon for these students
target_learners: university engineering-physics students in an introductory vector calculus course
target_learning_goals: interpreting and solving problems in vector calculus by integrating formulae, text, and graphical representations
examples: The study compared eight vector-calculus problems presented with or without lecturer-designed interpretational graphs, recording eye movements, think-aloud protocols, and correctness of confirm/reject decisions
key_sources: Ögren, M., Nyström, M., & Jarodzka, H. (2017). There's more to the multimedia effect than meets the eye: is seeing pictures believing? Instructional Science, 45, 263–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9397-6

citation: Matsuda, N., Cohen, W. W., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0020-1

description: CTAT is a suite of software tools that helps authors build Tutoring Interfaces with virtually no programming effort and demonstrate solutions stored as model solutions in a behavior graph. The system supports two authoring strategies, Authoring by Tutoring and Authoring by Demonstration, and also allows authors to demonstrate incorrect steps so SimStudent learns buggy production rules.

article_title: Measuring and Analyzing Students’ Strategic Learning Behaviors in Open-Ended Learning Environments
citation: Ningyu Zhang, Gautam Biswas, Nicole Hutchins. (2022). Measuring and Analyzing Students' Strategic Learning Behaviors in Open-Ended Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 32, 931–970. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00275-x
title: Task-oriented strategy framework for OELEs: strategies as conscious, controllable action sequences mapped to IA, SC, and SA cognitive processes
description: The framework defines strategies as "students’ conscious and controllable sequences of actions to facilitate and enhance task performance", making them measurable from log data. A hierarchical task model maps logged, time-stamped actions to three primary cognitive processes: Information Acquisition, Solution Construction, and Solution Assessment. Coherence Analysis plus sequence mining identify common action sequences interpreted as strategies, and differential sequence mining compares their use across performance groups. The authors state the framework generalizes prior Betty's Brain work and is applicable to other open-ended tasks that employ similar cognitive processes.
requirements: Learning environments must log students' activities in the context of the tasks they are performing for the analysis methods to be applied
constraints: The use of strategies is latent and cannot be observed or measured directly; it is only reflected in students' action sequences
target_learners: middle school students working in open-ended learning environments
target_learning_goals: science content learning
computational thinking practices
self-regulated learning strategies
examples: In the classroom study, students' logged actions were represented using a pre-defined <action,view> scheme, and sequence mining used an s-support threshold of 0.7 and a gap threshold of 6 minutes

article_title: Measuring and Analyzing Students’ Strategic Learning Behaviors in Open-Ended Learning Environments
citation: Ningyu Zhang, Gautam Biswas, Nicole Hutchins. (2022). Measuring and Analyzing Students' Strategic Learning Behaviors in Open-Ended Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 32, 931–970. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00275-x
title: CTSiM: a learning-by-modeling OELE for synergistic science and computational thinking learning
description: Computational Thinking using Simulation and Modeling (CTSiM) is an open-ended learning environment in which middle school students learn science by building conceptual and computational models. Students perform five primary tasks: reading a hypertext resource library, building conceptual models, constructing executable models with a block-based language, running simulations to debug behaviors, and comparing their model's behaviors to an expert reference model. Students have access to all interfaces at all times, which the authors say supports the open-ended nature of the approach. Units include kinematics, dynamics, diffusion, and ecology (fish tank).

constraints: The study omitted the collision unit from analyses because it served as preparation for the diffusion unit

title: Design-principle framework for CT-promoter e-learning environments: sequenced multiple representation, genuine active involvement, selective hiding, and pattern-recognition orientation
description: The article organizes its learning environment around four research-based design principles for promoting computational thinking. understanding sorting algorithms

description: The article proposes a developmental account (visualized in its Fig. 5) of how CT's cognitive correlates change across education levels. constraints: The study found no learning advantage for 360° VR over traditional media, so CTML-based predictions of superior outcomes were not supported

citation: Sukmojati E, Al Viana S, Kale Djami M, Fauzi A, Syafirah D, O.D. Bana E. (2025). Critical Thinking in English Language Teaching: A Bibliometric Analysis. F1000Research 14:1305. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.171160.1
title: Critical thinking as higher-order cognitive processes plus a disposition toward inquiry in ELT
description: The article frames critical thinking in English language teaching as involving higher-order cognitive processes and a dispositional component. Drawing on Davies and Barnett (2015), it states that "critical thinking involves the cultivation of higher-order cognitive processes such as analysis, evaluation, assessment, synthesis, and comparison" and that students "must not only acquire cognitive skills but also develop a mindset that encourages inquiry, innovation, and creativity." In ELT specifically, students are required to analyse the English language critically, reflecting on its structure, use and application in the construction of meaning. This framing underpins the article's argument that conventional instruction emphasising argumentation without deeper analytical engagement is insufficient.
requirements: Instruction that fosters both cognitive skills and a disposition toward inquiry, innovation and creativity
constraints: The article notes many ELT teachers have not yet developed the reflective competence needed to integrate critical thinking effectively, creating demand for professional development
target_learning_goals: Analysis, evaluation, synthesis and comparison of language and texts
Developing a disposition toward inquiry and creativity
examples: The article links this framing to Bloom's Revised Taxonomy, which emphasises higher-order thinking of analysis, evaluation and creation as core learning objectives

article_title: Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research.
citation: Lazarus Michelle D., Sarkar Mahbub, Palermo Claire, Soh Sze‐Ee, Farlie Melanie K. (2025). Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70053
title: Classical test theory and item response theory as psychometric approaches aligned with positivist and post-positivist worldviews respectively
description: The article presents CTT and IRT as two measurement theories whose assumptions map onto worldviews. CTT, the foundation of measurement theory "for over 80 years," models a test score as a true score plus random error, assumes the construct is stable and each person is "equal," and focuses analysis on total scores and reliability. IRT instead postulates that "a response to an item on a measurement tool is a function of the item's difficulty and the person's ability," enabling item-level difficulty and discrimination analysis; Rasch models further assume unidimensionality, local independence, and monotonicity.
requirements: CTT-developed scales require strong reliability and validity evidence before transfer across occasions and populations, and need revalidation in each new context of use
constraints: Not all latent trait model approaches assume unidimensionality; multivariate Rasch analysis may account for multiple influences on the desired construct
target_learning_goals: understanding how measurement theory assumptions relate to worldview commitments and to validity transferability
examples: The SAT is presented as a CTT-designed multidimensional test whose composite score cannot be read from a single item, and the APP as an IRT-developed scale
